reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A severe secondary glaucoma driven by new vessel growth on the iris (rubeosis iridis) and in the drainage angle in response to retinal ischaemia
The commonest underlying causes are ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease
Early rubeosis begins as fine vessels at the pupillary margin and angle before spreading; careful undilated gonioscopy and iris examination detect it before pressure rises
A fibrovascular membrane initially blocks the open angle, then contracts to pull the peripheral iris forward, producing progressive synechial (secondary) angle closure
Late presentation is with a painful red eye, very high intraocular pressure, corneal oedema, and poor vision, often with ectropion uveae from membrane contraction
Management targets the ischaemic drive with panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF injection, alongside topical pressure-lowering agents and control of pain and inflammation
Once the angle is extensively closed, drainage surgery with a tube or trabeculectomy, or a cyclodestructive procedure, is usually needed to control pressure
Identifying and treating the underlying retinal or carotid ischaemia is essential and may require systemic and vascular assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Neovascular glaucoma results from chronic retinal ischaemia, which triggers release of vascular endothelial growth factor and other angiogenic mediators into the aqueous. These stimulate growth of a fibrovascular membrane over the iris surface and across the trabecular meshwork. In the early open-angle phase this membrane physically covers and obstructs the meshwork, raising pressure while the angle still appears open on gonioscopy. As the membrane matures its myofibroblasts contract, dragging the peripheral iris anteriorly to form peripheral anterior synechiae and everting the pupil margin (ectropion uveae), which produces progressive synechial angle closure. The combination of outflow obstruction and secondary angle closure causes marked pressure elevation, corneal oedema, pain, and optic-nerve damage.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory (uveitic) glaucoma with anterior segment vessels
Chronic angle-closure glaucoma from other causes
Fuchs heterochromic uveitis with fine iris vessels
Post-traumatic or ghost cell glaucoma with a red painful eye
additionalInvestigations: Undilated slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy to detect early rubeosis and angle new vessels
Applanation tonometry to gauge the pressure rise
Dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging or fluorescein angiography to identify the ischaemic driver
Carotid Doppler or vascular imaging when ocular ischaemic syndrome is suspected
Assessment and control of systemic diabetes and cardiovascular risk factors
B-scan ultrasonography when media opacity obscures the retina
redFlags: New iris or angle vessels signalling active retinal ischaemia that demands urgent treatment before the angle closes
Painful red eye with very high pressure and corneal oedema requiring emergency care
An ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion or proliferative diabetic retinopathy known to precede rubeosis
Ocular ischaemic syndrome pointing to significant carotid disease and systemic vascular risk
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on how early the neovascular drive is treated; caught at the rubeosis stage, panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF therapy may regress vessels and preserve the angle, but established synechial closure often leaves a difficult-to-control eye with poor visual potential, and some eyes become painful and blind despite treatment.
pitfalls: Dilating the pupil before examining for early rubeosis and missing angle new vessels
Treating the pressure alone without addressing the underlying retinal or carotid ischaemia
Relying on anti-VEGF injection, whose effect is temporary, without definitive panretinal photocoagulation
Delaying treatment until the angle has already closed synechially
Overlooking ocular ischaemic syndrome and an underlying carotid stenosis
management: Ablate the ischaemic retinal drive with panretinal photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-VEGF injection to regress the fibrovascular membrane
Lower intraocular pressure with topical agents such as beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, adding systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or hyperosmotics for acute rises
Relieve pain and inflammation with topical corticosteroid and cycloplegic drops
Proceed to glaucoma drainage (tube or valve) surgery or a cyclodestructive procedure for pressure uncontrolled medically once synechial angle closure is established

Identify and treat the underlying cause, whether ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion, proliferative diabetic retinopathy or carotid ocular ischaemic syndrome, including carotid intervention where indicated
Detect early rubeosis with undilated gonioscopy and iris examination and treat before pressure rises to preserve the angle
Monitor intraocular pressure and, in a blind painful eye, consider palliative measures for comfort
